stem: A logistics-scheduling agent has kept an unused shipment-cancellation tool for six months. Ahead of the annual SOC 2 audit, the compliance lead's plan is to keep the tool active and log every invocation. What should replace this plan?

opts.t: Keep the tool active and route every invocation to a SIEM alert the compliance lead reviews before the audit.
Keep the tool, but require a supervisor's confirmation before each cancellation executes.
Remove the shipment-cancellation tool from the agent's toolset; six months of production use confirms the task never required it.
Route cancellation requests through a separate approval service that validates and executes them outside the agent's direct control.

whyRight: Six months of unused access with no legitimate need means the failure class can be eliminated rather than mitigated. Logging only records misuse after it happens; removing the tool takes away the capability a cancellation error would require, the strongest and cheapest control available here.

whyWrong.A: A SIEM alert only detects a cancellation after it executes; logging is appropriate when misuse is low-consequence and reversible, not for an unused, unassessed tool.
whyWrong.B: A supervisor's confirmation still leaves the tool and its capability in place, and the safeguard's strength depends entirely on how carefully that confirmation is given each time.
whyWrong.D: A separate approval service fits a tool still needed occasionally; this tool has gone unused six months, so the task needs no such capability at all.

t1Clause: kept an unused shipment-cancellation tool for six months

stem: A RAG assistant serving 5,000 daily support tickets began giving confident, incorrect answers this week. The knowledge corpus was reindexed Monday, and the model provider also rolled out a routine version update the same day. Select two correct first diagnostic steps.

opts.t: Investigate the retrieval pipeline — chunk boundaries, embedding version, and index freshness — for errors traceable to Monday's reindex.
Insert deterministic validation checkpoints between each step of the support pipeline to interrupt any compounding across steps.
Add an instruction to the system prompt directing the assistant to only answer from verified, high-confidence context.
Check the pinned model version against the prior release and run the regression set for the vendor's update.

whyRight: Two changes landed the same day, so both must be ruled in or out. The reindex timing points at the retrieval pipeline — chunking, embedding version, index freshness — while the concurrent vendor update requires checking the pinned model version and regression set before either cause is ruled out.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the stem describes a multi-step chain where each step passes its own test yet the combined result is worse; that failure mode is not in evidence here.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction to only use verified context patches the model's output, not the two concurrent changes; it does nothing to check the reindex or the vendor's version update.

t1Clause: The knowledge corpus was reindexed Monday, and the model provider also rolled out a routine version update the same day

stem: A fraud-flagging assistant commits to a 2-minute customer response SLA, and leadership wants every flagged transaction reviewed by a human before action. At current volume, full human review cannot finish inside that window. Which policy should the team adopt?

opts.t: Keep full human review of every flagged transaction, and add reviewers on rotation to try to meet the 2-minute window.
Auto-approve high-confidence, low-severity flags within the window; route flags above a stated threshold to human review, even past the SLA.
Remove the human-review requirement and let the assistant auto-approve every flagged transaction to guarantee the SLA.
Review a random sample of flagged transactions each hour and auto-approve the rest to stay within the SLA.

whyRight: A hard 2-minute SLA and full human review of every flag cannot both hold at this volume, so the team has to name which one binds. Auto-approving low-severity, high-confidence flags inside the window while routing everything above a stated threshold states that trade rather than hiding it.

whyWrong.A: Adding reviewers does not make a fraud review take under two minutes; full review of every item is correct only for genuinely low-volume, high-consequence work, not this stated volume.
whyWrong.C: Removing human review entirely satisfies only the SLA and abandons the stated regulatory expectation; the binding constraint is the confidence-and-severity threshold, not a blanket removal of oversight.
whyWrong.D: Uniform hourly sampling reviews flags in proportion to how often they occur, not their severity, so the costliest flags are no more likely to reach a reviewer.

t1Clause: full human review cannot finish inside that window
lessonKey: above approve auto confidence even flags high human low past review route severity sla stated threshold window within

stem: A payments platform enforces PCI cardholder-data-environment isolation, blocking any service outside that boundary from querying it directly. A new fraud-analytics workload needs narrow, logged access to tokenized, non-cardholder transaction metadata only, pending compliance review. What should the team add?

opts.t: A scoped exception at the infrastructure layer permitting only the named records and region, logged and time-bound.
Remove the data-residency control for this integration's traffic so the partner can pull the records directly.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model never to return records outside the approved region.
Commission a third-party compliance audit of the entire data-residency architecture before allowing any cross-region exception.

whyRight: Data residency is enforced at the infrastructure layer because the requirement is absolute, and a legitimate new need does not change that. A scoped, logged, time-bound exception at the same layer grants the access needed without loosening the boundary or moving enforcement into a prompt.

whyWrong.B: Removing the control for this traffic reopens the exposure the boundary exists to prevent; a narrow legitimate need calls for a scoped exception, not for lifting the boundary itself.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction fits a preference, not an absolute residency requirement; it is evaluated after the model already holds the records and depends on the model complying.
whyWrong.D: A full architecture audit answers a broader question than this request and delays a narrow, already-scoped access need without changing whether the boundary itself is sound.

t1Clause: enforces EU data-residency at the infrastructure layer
lessonKey: bound exception infrastructure layer logged named only permitting records region scoped time

stem: To meet a compliance deadline without building new logging, an audit lead proposes having the model generate a short explanation attached to every declined application, to serve as the audit record for regulators. What is the correct next step?

opts.t: Provide the generated explanation to declined applicants for their own understanding, and file it as the audit record too.
Keep the generated explanation as the audit record, and add a disclaimer noting it may not be fully accurate.
Commission an independent model audit to certify the explanation generator's overall reliability before regulators review any decisions.
Remove the generated explanation as the audit record, and log the inputs, evidence, versions, and threshold behind each decision.

whyRight: A generated rationale is confidently wrong about its own causes exactly when it matters most, so it cannot serve as evidence of what happened. Removing it from the audit role and logging the inputs, evidence, versions, and threshold that actually produced each decision reconstructs the real path regulators need.

whyWrong.A: Handing the explanation to applicants is fine, but filing that same generated text as the regulator's audit record is what the section rules out.
whyWrong.B: A disclaimer describes the record's limits without changing what it is; the audit still rests on text produced after the fact, not a trace of what happened.
whyWrong.C: Certifying the generator's general reliability answers a different question than what determined this specific decision, and the compliance deadline does not allow time for an independent audit anyway.

t1Clause: to serve as the audit record for regulators

stem: An internal reporting agent holds a tool that can permanently delete customer records, though its stated task is read-only summarization. The security lead added invocation logging and asks whether that satisfies the least-privilege requirement before sign-off.

opts.t: Confirm the existing invocation logging and monthly audit review satisfy the least-privilege requirement.
Require a second engineer's sign-off before each delete-tool invocation executes.
Move the delete tool to a scoped service account with tighter database permissions and continuous monitoring.
Remove the delete tool from the agent's tool definitions, since the task does not need it.

whyRight: Least privilege is satisfied by removing a capability the task does not need, not by monitoring its use. Deleting the delete tool eliminates the failure class entirely, while logging, sign-off, and scoped permissions only detect or narrow a capability that should not exist.

whyWrong.A: Logging and periodic audit review record misuse after it happens; they do not stop the deletion from executing, which is the audit misconception this section corrects.
whyWrong.B: A second-engineer sign-off is a partial gate that still leaves the delete capability available and depends on whoever grants the approval.
whyWrong.C: A scoped service account and tighter permissions still preserve a delete capability the task never required; thorough permissioning is not the same as removing it.

t1Clause: its stated task is read-only summarization

stem: Finance requires that every extracted payment amount match its source invoice before an assistant approves 12,000 monthly payments, and asks which verification step reliably catches figures the model transcribed incorrectly.

opts.t: Have the same model re-read the invoice and re-confirm the extracted figure without external comparison.
Compare every extracted figure against the invoice's original structured field before the payment posts.
Route the extraction through a second, independently trained model and post only when both agree.
Manually verify a random five percent sample of approved payments each week for accuracy.

whyRight: Comparing every extracted figure against the invoice's own structured field is a deterministic check that fails independently of the model's generation process, matching the section's rule that only a check drawn from outside the model reliably catches confident, incorrect figures.

whyWrong.A: A second read by the same model shares its generation process and failure mode; asking a model to re-check itself is not independent verification.
whyWrong.C: Two independently trained models can still share correlated training data and agree while both are wrong, so agreement is not equivalent to independent evidence.
whyWrong.D: Finance requires every figure caught before approval; a weekly five-percent sample lets most mismatches post before anyone reviews them.

t1Clause: every extracted payment amount match its source invoice

stem: A federal agency's FedRAMP authorization confines every workload to its approved environment. A project drafting marketing copy from public press releases, touching no protected data, faces a six-week queue to enter that environment, and the program office asks how to proceed.

opts.t: Grant a scoped, reviewed exception for this specific low-risk workload, leaving the general authorized-environment requirement intact.
Relax the authorized-environment requirement generally so future public-data workloads can bypass the queue without individual review.
Require the marketing project to wait in the standard authorization queue like every other workload, regardless of content.
Let the model classify each output as public or sensitive, routing sensitive content to the authorized environment.

whyRight: The authorized-environment requirement is correctly enforced for regulated data; a workload that genuinely touches none of it can be carved out through its own scoped, reviewed exception, which preserves the boundary for every workload that does need it.

whyWrong.B: Relaxing the requirement generally reopens the environment boundary for future workloads that may touch protected data, undoing the protection the authorization exists to provide.
whyWrong.C: The workload touches no protected data; the queue exists to control that category, so forcing an identical wait ignores the stated risk difference.
whyWrong.D: A model-side classifier is probabilistic; whenever it misclassifies, regulated content would reach an environment the authorization was never granted for.

lessonKey: authorized environment exception general grant intact leaving low requirement reviewed risk scoped specific workload

stem: A hiring-screening model cannot equalize its selection rate and false-negative rate across two demographic groups because their base rates differ. The model risk committee, already using a stratified equal-N sample, must decide how to proceed before the next audit.

opts.t: Escalate to legal counsel without specifying which fairness definition will govern the model going forward.
Continue retraining until both parity constraints are satisfied at the same threshold.
Decide which harm the model must avoid, select the matching fairness definition, and document the rationale.
Rebalance the evaluation sample to equal N per group, since the smaller group's sample size is driving the conflict.

whyRight: Equal selection rate and equal false-negative rate cannot both hold when base rates differ, so the resolution is a stated choice: name the harm being controlled, select the fairness definition that controls it, and record the rationale for the audit trail.

whyWrong.A: Escalating without naming a fairness definition leaves the conflict unresolved and produces no documented rationale for the audit.
whyWrong.B: Base rates already differ, so retraining toward both parity constraints at once chases a target the section says cannot generally be reached.
whyWrong.D: The sample is already stratified with equal N per group, so rebalancing again does not address why the two metrics conflict; base rates differ instead.

t1Clause: already using a stratified equal-N sample
lessonKey: being choose controlled harm rationale record which
